Jump to any section — all entries are equal size 📖 Introduction 🚀 Why Learn This 🌍 Significance ➕ Arithmetic ⚖️ Comparison 🔀 Logical ✏️ Assignment 💻 Bitwise 🔍 Membership 🆔 Identity 📊 Precedence ❓ FAQ 💛 Outro Perform mathematical operations on numbers. Python supports all standard arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, //, %, **. Step 1: Addition: 10 + 3 adds two numbers. Step 2: Subtraction: 10 - 3 subtracts the second from the first. Step 3: Multiplication: 10 * 3 multiplies two numbers. Step 4: Division: 10 / 3 returns a float. Step 5: Floor division: 10 // 3 returns the integer quotient. Step 6: Modulo: 10 % 3 returns the remainder. Step 7: Exponentiation: 10 ** 3 raises to a power. python Copy Run a, b = 10, 3 print(f"a + b = {a + b}") print(f"a - b = {a - b}") print(f"a * b = {a * b}") print(f"a / b = {a / b}") print(f"a // b = {a // b}") print(f"a % b = {a % b}") print(f"a ** b = {a ** b}") 💡 Division / always returns a float. Use // for integer division. The modulo operator returns the remainder of a division. It's useful for checking divisibility and cycling through ranges. Step 1: Check if a number is even: num % 2 == 0. Step 2: Get the last digit: num % 10. Step 3: Cycle through a range: index % 3 gives 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2... python Copy Run num = 17 print(f"num % 2 = {num % 2}") print(f"{num} is even: {num % 2 == 0}") print(f"num % 10 = {num % 10}") for i in range(6): print(f"{i} % 3 = {i % 3}") Compare values and return True or False. Python supports: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=. Step 1: Equal to: x == y checks if values are equal. Step 2: Not equal: x != y checks if values are different. Step 3: Greater than: x > y. Step 4: Less than: x < y. Step 5: Greater than or equal to: x >= y. Step 6: Less than or equal to: x <= y. python Copy Run x, y = 5, 10 print(f"x == y: {x == y}") print(f"x != y: {x != y}") print(f"x > y: {x > y}") print(f"x < y: {x < y}") print(f"x >= y: {x >= y}") print(f"x <= y: {x <= y}") 💡 Comparison operators are used in if statements and loops to control program flow. Python allows chaining comparisons: a < b < c is equivalent to a < b and b < c. Step 1: Chain comparisons for cleaner code. Step 2: Check if a value is within a range. python Copy Run x = 5 print(f"1 < x < 10: {1 < x < 10}") print(f"0 <= x <= 10: {0 <= x <= 10}") print(f"(1 < x) and (x < 10): {(1 < x) and (x < 10)}") Combine boolean values: and, or, not. Logical operators are used to combine conditional statements. Step 1: and returns True if both operands are true. Step 2: or returns True if at least one operand is true. Step 3: not returns the opposite boolean value. python Copy Run a, b = True, False print(f"a and b: {a and b}") print(f"a or b: {a or b}") print(f"not a: {not a}") x, y = 5, 10 print(f"x > 3 and y < 20: {x > 3 and y < 20}") print(f"x > 10 or y > 5: {x > 10 or y > 5}") 💡 Logical operators short-circuit: and stops at the first False, or stops at the first True. Assign values to variables, often combined with arithmetic. Python supports: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, //=, **=. Step 1: x = 10 assigns the value 10. Step 2: x += 5 is equivalent to x = x + 5. Step 3: x *= 2 is equivalent to x = x * 2. python Copy Run x = 10 print(f"x = {x}") x += 3 print(f"x += 3 → x = {x}") x -= 5 print(f"x -= 5 → x = {x}") x *= 2 print(f"x *= 2 → x = {x}") x /= 4 print(f"x /= 4 → x = {x}") x //= 2 print(f"x //= 2 → x = {x}") x **= 2 print(f"x **= 2 → x = {x}") Work with numbers at the binary level: &, |, ^, ~, <<, >>. Bitwise operators are used for low-level manipulation of integer bits. Step 1: & (AND): 1 if both bits are 1. Step 2: | (OR): 1 if at least one bit is 1. Step 3: ^ (XOR): 1 if bits are different. Step 4: ~ (NOT): Inverts all bits. Step 5: << (Left shift): Shifts bits left. Step 6: >> (Right shift): Shifts bits right. python Copy Run a, b = 6, 3 print(f"a = {a} (binary: {bin(a)})") print(f"b = {b} (binary: {bin(b)})") print(f"a & b = {a & b} ({bin(a & b)})") print(f"a | b = {a | b} ({bin(a | b)})") print(f"a ^ b = {a ^ b} ({bin(a ^ b)})") print(f"~a = {~a} ({bin(~a)})") print(f"a << 1 = {a << 1} ({bin(a << 1)})") print(f"a >> 1 = {a >> 1} ({bin(a >> 1)})") Bitwise operators are commonly used to manage flags and permissions. Step 1: Define flags: READ = 1, WRITE = 2, EXEC = 4. Step 2: Combine flags using |: READ | WRITE. Step 3: Check if a flag is set using &. python Copy Run READ = 1 WRITE = 2 EXEC = 4 permissions = READ | WRITE print(f"permissions: {permissions} (binary: {bin(permissions)})") if permissions & READ: print("Read permission granted") if permissions & WRITE: print("Write permission granted") if permissions & EXEC: print("Execute permission granted") else: print("Execute permission NOT granted") Check if a value exists in a sequence: in, not in. Membership operators are used to test if a value is present in a list, tuple, string, or other collection. Step 1: in returns True if the value is found. Step 2: not in returns True if the value is not found. python Copy Run fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] print(f"'apple' in fruits: {'apple' in fruits}") print(f"'grape' in fruits: {'grape' in fruits}") print(f"'grape' not in fruits: {'grape' not in fruits}") text = "Hello, world!" print(f"'world' in text: {'world' in text}") print(f"'Python' in text: {'Python' in text}") Compare object identity: is, is not. Identity operators check if two variables refer to the same object in memory. Step 1: is returns True if both variables point to the same object. Step 2: is not returns True if they point to different objects. Step 3: == compares values, is compares identity. python Copy Run a = [1, 2, 3] b = a c = [1, 2, 3] print(f"a = {a}, id(a): {id(a)}") print(f"b = {b}, id(b): {id(b)}") print(f"c = {c}, id(c): {id(c)}") print(f"a is b: {a is b}") print(f"a is c: {a is c}") print(f"a == c: {a == c}") x = 10 y = 10 print(f"x is y (integers): {x is y}") ⚠️ Use is for None, booleans, and checking object identity. Use == for value comparisons. Python follows specific rules to determine the order in which operators are evaluated. Use parentheses to make your code explicit and avoid confusion. Step 1: Exponentiation has the highest precedence among arithmetic operators. Step 2: Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction. Step 3: Comparison operators have lower precedence than arithmetic. Step 4: Logical operators have lower precedence than comparisons. Step 5: Use parentheses to override default precedence. python Copy Run print("Without parentheses:") print(f"10 + 5 * 2 = {10 + 5 * 2}") print(f"(10 + 5) * 2 = {(10 + 5) * 2}") print("\nComparison and logical:") x, y, z = 5, 10, 15 print(f"x < y and y < z: {x < y and y < z}") print(f"x < y and y > z: {x < y and y > z}") print(f"x < y or y > z: {x < y or y > z}") 💡 When in doubt, use parentheses! They make your intention clear and improve readability. Common questions about operators in Python, answered. + == compares the values of two objects, while is checks if they refer to the same object in memory. Use == for value equality, and is for identity (e.g., None). + The modulo operator % returns the remainder of a division. For example, 10 % 3 returns 1. It's useful for checking divisibility, cycling through ranges, and extracting digits. + Bitwise operators work at the binary level. They are used for low-level programming, flag manipulation, permissions, packing data, and optimization. + Operator precedence determines the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression. For example, multiplication is evaluated before addition. Use parentheses to override the default precedence. + In logical expressions, Python stops evaluating as soon as the result is known. For and, if the first operand is False, it doesn't evaluate the second. For or, if the first operand is True, it doesn't evaluate the second. + Yes! + concatenates strings, * repeats strings, and in checks for substring membership. Comparison operators work lexicographically. + / performs floating-point division and always returns a float. // performs floor division and returns the integer quotient, discarding the remainder.
